planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into moist to wet, humus-rich tallgrass prairie or sedge-meadow soil in partial shade; never dig from the wild, as this is a federally threatened species — source only certified propagated stock.

directions: Eastern prairie fringed orchid produces a stout spike of up to forty large, creamy-white, deeply fringed flowers in late June and July, each releasing a strong sweet fragrance after dusk to attract its night-flying sphinx moth pollinators. It is a federally threatened relic of Midwestern tallgrass prairie, sedge meadows, and fens, where it depends on periodic fire or mowing to keep woody competitors from shading out its sunny, consistently moist habitat. The fleshy tuberous root requires intact native mycorrhizal fungi, so transplanting is rarely successful outside specialized prairie-restoration or botanic-garden settings. A true connoisseur's conservation plant rather than a casual garden subject, best attempted only through ethically propagated nursery stock in a restored wet prairie planting.

planting.note: Plant certified nursery-propagated tubers in spring into moist, calcareous tallgrass-prairie or wet sedge-meadow soil with full sun exposure softened by surrounding tall grasses; this federally threatened species should never be wild-collected.

directions: Western prairie fringed orchid bears up to two dozen large, pale greenish-white, heavily fringed flowers on a single stalk in June and July, with a longer nectar spur and bigger blooms than its eastern relative, and a strong nocturnal fragrance that lures large sphinx moths. It survives today mostly on remnant Great Plains tallgrass prairie and moist swales from Minnesota and the Dakotas south to Kansas and Nebraska, habitat that has shrunk drastically with conversion to cropland and fire suppression. Like other Platanthera, it depends on specific mycorrhizal fungi and resents root disturbance, making it a subject for prairie-restoration specialists rather than typical home gardens. Conservation organizations across the northern Great Plains actively protect remaining populations through controlled burns and haying regimes that mimic historic prairie disturbance.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into consistently moist, rich soil along a streambank or moist woodland-edge planting in partial shade; avoid wild collection and keep soil from drying out.

directions: Purple fringeless orchid sends up a dense spike of rich magenta-purple flowers with shallowly fringed, unlobed lips in mid to late summer, a showier and less finely cut relative of the yellow fringed orchids. It occurs naturally in moist bottomland forests, wet meadows, marsh edges, and streambanks through the Mid-Atlantic, Ohio Valley, and Ozark regions, usually in dappled light at a woodland margin rather than deep shade. The clearwing hummingbird moth is its primary pollinator, drawn to the nectar-rich spur on each flower. Give it steady moisture and humus-rich soil at a stream edge or rain-garden margin, and avoid letting the site dry out during the growing season.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring in deep, cool, moist forest duff under a closed deciduous or mixed canopy; the pair of flat basal leaves should lie directly on the humus surface, undisturbed by mulching.

directions: Round-leaved orchid forms a distinctive pair of broad, nearly circular, glossy leaves pressed flat against the forest floor, from which a slender stalk of small, loosely spaced greenish-white flowers rises in midsummer. It ranges across cool, moist, mature forests from Alaska and most of Canada south through New England, the Appalachians, the Great Lakes region, and the Rocky Mountains, always under a closed canopy with deep leaf litter. Like most native terrestrial orchids it depends on specific mycorrhizal fungi present in undisturbed forest soil, so success depends on transplanting with surrounding native duff intact rather than bare-root planting. Best suited to a shaded native woodland garden left largely undisturbed, where its sculptural paired leaves provide interest even when not in flower.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in cool, consistently moist, mossy soil under coniferous or mixed-forest canopy in shade; this boreal species needs cold winters and will not tolerate warm, dry summer sites.

directions: Blunt-leaved orchid is a diminutive boreal species with a single rounded, blunt-tipped basal leaf and a short spike of small greenish-white flowers, unusual among orchids in being pollinated chiefly by mosquitoes along with a few other small insects. It grows in cold, mossy coniferous and mixed forests and bogs across much of Canada, Alaska, and the northern tier of the Lower 48, often alongside sphagnum and feather mosses in shaded, saturated ground. Because it is adapted to short, cool growing seasons and acidic, perpetually moist substrate, it is essentially unsuited to typical garden conditions outside northern bog-garden or native-plant conservation collections. Provide shaded, evenly moist, mossy soil and cold winters, and expect it to remain a specialist's plant rather than a mainstream perennial.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into wet, acidic, peaty soil in a bog garden or seepage-slope planting with partial shade; keep the site saturated through the growing season as in its native savanna habitat.

directions: Yellow fringeless orchid produces a compact spike of golden-yellow flowers with shallowly fringed, unlobed lips in mid to late summer, smaller and more unified in color than the showier orange-crested species it grows alongside. It is native to open wet savannas and bogs of the southeastern coastal plain from eastern Texas to North Carolina, with scattered disjunct populations as far north as New Jersey, always in consistently saturated, acidic, peaty or sandy soil. Fire-maintained open wetlands keep competing woody vegetation at bay, so a cultivated bog garden should mimic that open, sunny-but-moist structure with light shade at the margins. Source only nursery-propagated plants, as wild populations are vulnerable to habitat drainage and fire suppression.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring along a seasonally flooded shoreline, wet meadow, or rain-garden margin in partial shade; this northern variety depends on periodic natural disturbance such as ice scour to keep its site open.

directions: Tubercled rein orchid, the northern variety of the pale-green or southern rein orchid, bears a dense, somewhat inconspicuous spike of small yellowish-green flowers from midsummer into early fall, each lip bearing the small raised tubercle that gives the plant its name. It favors seasonally flooded shorelines of lakes and rivers and wet meadows across the Great Lakes region and northeastern North America, where natural ice scour or periodic flooding keeps the vegetation open rather than closing in with shrubs. Plant it in a consistently damp rain-garden or pond-margin setting with loose, organically rich soil and partial shade from nearby trees. As with other native terrestrial orchids, rely on nursery-propagated stock, since the species depends on an intact mycorrhizal association that bare-root wild-dug plants rarely survive transplanting without.

planting.note: Plant only certified nursery-propagated stock in spring in deep leaf litter under a mature hardwood or mixed conifer-hardwood canopy near an intermittent stream; never disturb or collect wild plants, as this is a federally threatened species.

directions: Small whorled pogonia is a rare and elusive terrestrial orchid bearing a single waxy gray-green stem topped by a whorl of five or six gray-green leaves and one or two small, pale yellow-green flowers in late spring. It inhabits deep leaf litter in hardwood and mixed conifer-hardwood forests, often near intermittent streams, from Maine south to Georgia and west to the Great Lakes, with populations so sparse and cryptic that plants can remain dormant underground for years between visible shoot emergence. Federally listed as threatened, it is highly sensitive to disturbance, canopy change, and soil compaction, and essentially cannot be successfully transplanted or propagated outside specialized conservation programs. Any garden use should be limited strictly to documented ex-situ conservation collections rather than ordinary landscaping, with absolute protection of leaf litter and soil structure.
sources: New England Wild Flower Society (Native Plant Trust)

planting.note: Transfer divisions of the coral-like rhizome in early spring with a generous amount of surrounding native forest soil to preserve the fungal partners the plant depends on entirely; plant in undisturbed, moist, humus-rich duff under a closed canopy.

directions: Early coralroot is a small, pale yellowish-green orchid that is only partially myco-heterotrophic, retaining a little chlorophyll of its own in addition to the nutrients it draws from fungal partners in the soil. It has one of the widest distributions of any orchid, occurring circumboreally across North America, Europe, and much of temperate and boreal Asia in cool, moist, often calcareous forest soils. It blooms earliest of the coralroots, often in late spring while deciduous leaf canopy is still thin, producing a short spike of small greenish-yellow flowers. Because of its partial reliance on soil fungi, it establishes best when transplanted with intact native duff rather than as a bare-root division, and it is best treated as a passive presence in an undisturbed native woodland planting rather than a plant to be actively managed.

planting.note: Transfer small rhizome divisions in late summer or early fall with attached native soil into undisturbed forest duff under a closed canopy; this species flowers in autumn and should not be disturbed once in bud.

directions: Autumn coralroot is a small, leafless, chlorophyll-free orchid with a yellowish-brown stem bulbous at the base, producing tiny reddish-purple flowers with a white, purple-spotted lip from August into October, well after most other woodland wildflowers have finished blooming. It is widespread in forested areas across the eastern and central United States and into Mexico and Central America, deriving all of its nutrition from soil fungi rather than photosynthesis, and some plants never fully open their flowers, instead self-pollinating in the bud. Its complete dependence on mycorrhizal fungi makes successful transplanting difficult, so it is best left undisturbed where it appears naturally in a mature woodland garden with intact leaf litter. Mark its location in fall so the dormant, nearly invisible plant is not disturbed during the rest of the year.

planting.note: Transfer rhizome divisions in early spring with surrounding native duff into undisturbed, decaying leaf and needle litter beneath pine or mixed coniferous forest; success depends entirely on intact native fungal associations.

directions: Striped coralroot sends up an erect, leafless, reddish to nearly white stem bearing pink or yellowish flowers boldly striped with darker purple veining, among the showiest of the chlorophyll-free coralroots. It grows scattered through dry, decaying litter on the floor of pine and mixed coniferous forests from Alberta and British Columbia south through the western United States to Mexico, relying entirely on mycoheterotrophic fungal partnerships since it has no roots or leaves of its own. Because it cannot photosynthesize, it may remain invisible underground for years between flowering seasons, making its appearance unpredictable even in suitable habitat. It is not a plant that can be reliably cultivated or increased by normal gardening methods; at best it can be protected in place within an undisturbed coniferous woodland planting that preserves its native soil fungi.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in a fine, open bark-based or humus-rich woodland mix in partial to full shade; keep warm (around 68-85F) and evenly moist, bringing containers indoors or under cover where winters drop below the mid-20s F.

directions: Tall rattlesnake plantain is an evergreen terrestrial orchid with plain, unpatterned dark green leaves (unlike the silver-netted leaves of many related Goodyera) and an erect spike of small white flowers rising well above the foliage. Widespread across subtropical and tropical Asia from China and Japan through India and Southeast Asia, it grows terrestrially in humus-rich, well-drained woodland litter in warm, shaded forest settings. In cultivation it thrives in an open, fast-draining mix of fine bark and leaf mold kept consistently moist but never waterlogged, and it does not creep or spread aggressively, forming a slowly increasing clump instead. Protect it from temperatures much below freezing, making it best suited to warm-temperate and subtropical shade gardens or a protected woodland terrarium elsewhere.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in deep to partial shade under a deciduous or mixed canopy; a loose leaf-litter mulch helps conserve moisture around the rosette.

directions: Japanese rattlesnake plantain forms a low evergreen rosette of dark green leaves marked with a fine network of pale venation, from which a slender spike of small, hooded, whitish flowers emerges in late summer to early fall. It is native to forested hillsides and woodland floors across China, Japan, and Korea, growing in the same kind of cool, humus-rich, well-drained shaded soil favored by its North American relatives such as downy rattlesnake plantain. In the garden it slowly forms small colonies through short rhizomes and makes an attractive textured groundcover for a shaded rock garden or woodland bed. Give it consistent moisture without waterlogging and protect the evergreen rosettes from being buried under heavy leaf drop in fall.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring into consistently wet, calcareous fen or bog-garden soil in partial shade; an even, year-round water supply is essential, as this species cannot tolerate drying out.

directions: Fen orchid, also called Loesel's twayblade or yellow widelip orchid, is a tiny, easily overlooked wetland orchid with two or three fleshy, tongue-like leaves at its base and a short spike of five to ten small, yellow-green flowers in early to midsummer. It grows in calcareous fens, bogs, and dune slacks across Europe, northern Asia, and the eastern United States and Canada, always in ground that stays evenly saturated, since even brief drying can be fatal. The species has already gone extinct in several European locations due to wetland drainage, and surviving populations are intensively monitored and protected, making nursery-propagated material essential for any cultivation. It is best suited to a dedicated calcareous bog or fen garden with a reliable year-round water table rather than an ordinary perennial border.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into deep, sharply drained sandy soil in open pine-oak woodland with dappled shade; avoid rich garden soil or heavy mulch, which encourages rot.

directions: Sandhills pyxie-moss is a tiny, mat-forming evergreen subshrub with needle-like leaves densely woolly on their undersides and an abundance of small white to pale pink star-shaped flowers that blanket the mat in early spring. Known only from deep, sandy ridgetops and sandhill woodlands of North Carolina and South Carolina, it closely resembles its more widespread relative Pyxidanthera barbulata but has shorter, hairless-margined leaves, and is treated as a distinct species by multiple botanical authorities. It thrives in the same sharply drained, nutrient-poor sandy soil under open pine-oak canopy that defines the fire-maintained longleaf pine sandhill ecosystem, and resents rich soil, excess moisture, or heavy mulch. Best used as a specialty groundcover in a sandhill-themed rock garden or native-plant collection with excellent drainage and light shade.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in full to partial shade under conifers; keep consistently moist through the first growing season.

directions: Wagner's wild ginger is a regional endemic of the Siskiyou Mountains of southwestern Oregon and northern California, forming a low, slowly spreading mat of heart-shaped, matte green leaves close to the ground in moist, shaded conifer forest. Its small, maroon, urn-shaped flowers are hidden at the base of the foliage where they are pollinated by ground-dwelling insects, following the same cryptic pollination strategy as other Asarum species. It is closely related to and sometimes confused with the more widespread Asarum caudatum, but remains more geographically restricted and less commonly offered commercially. In cultivation it prefers the cool, humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil of its native range, making it a good choice for Pacific Northwest shade gardens seeking regional native groundcover diversity beyond the common wild gingers.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in full to partial shade; mulch lightly with leaf litter to keep roots cool and evenly moist.

directions: Manchurian wild ginger is a cold-hardy East Asian wild ginger native to forested slopes of northeastern China, Korea, and the Russian Far East, forming a low clump of heart-shaped, deciduous leaves over a thick aromatic rhizome. Its variety mandshuricum is well known as the source of the traditional Chinese and Korean medicinal root commonly called xi xin, long used in East Asian herbal medicine, distinguishing it from the closely related but separately documented Asarum sieboldii. As a garden plant it performs much like other temperate wild gingers, spreading slowly to form a modest shaded groundcover in rich, consistently moist woodland soil. It tolerates colder winters than many ornamental Asian Asarum species, making it a useful hardy option for continental climates seeking an East Asian counterpart to native North American wild gingers.
